neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, fully oriented. Appears unperturbed by the arrest and shows marked indifference to wife's visible distress. Speech fluent and grammatically intact, normal prosody. No word-finding pauses. Repeated joking about the shoplifting incident with no appreciation of its seriousness. Denied any memory problems or behavioral changes. Brief cognitive screen in ED: MMSE 27/30 (loses 1 on serial-7s, 1 on recall, 1 on a complex command); Montreal Cognitive Assessment could not be completed in full ED setting, estimated frontal subscale severely reduced (clock drawing: poor planning, numerals crowded to the right; trails B failed on first attempt).

neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone. Strength 5/5 throughout. No tremor. No rigidity. Bilateral palmomental reflex present. Snout reflex present. Grasp reflex absent.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffman sign.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact finger-nose bilaterally. Normal rapid alternating movements.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence, stride, and arm swing. No parkinsonian features.
neurological_exam.additional: Wife history (patient denies everything): Over approximately 18 months, Mr. R has progressively changed personality. He was formerly punctual, conscientious, and warmly regarded at work. His wife describes three core changes: (1) Apathy and loss of initiative — stopped engaging with family activities, rarely initiates conversation, no longer interested in cooking (a prior hobby). (2) Loss of empathy — she cried at her mother's funeral and he laughed; he no longer recognizes emotional cues in children or friends. (3) Disinhibition and poor judgment — made an unauthorized $6,000 wire transfer to a foreign online casino; made sexually inappropriate comments to a neighbor; has taken small items from stores on at least three prior occasions, which the family covered up. (4) Dietary change — craves sweet foods almost exclusively; gained 14 lbs without explanation. (5) Repetitive behavior — watches the same two action films on a daily loop; arranges shoes in the same pattern each morning. The current ED presentation followed arrest for shoplifting a $29 bottle of cognac from a supermarket. The family had attributed the behavioral changes to work stress and then to grief after he lost his job, which delayed help-seeking by approximately a year. No recent fever, headache, neck stiffness, or focal neurological symptoms reported.

patient.chief_complaint: 61-year-old man brought to ED by police and wife after arrest for shoplifting; wife reports 18-month behavioral deterioration
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. R is a 61-year-old Hispanic man with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia who is brought to the emergency department by police officers and his wife following an arrest for shoplifting a bottle of cognac at a local supermarket. He has no prior psychiatric history. He is fully cooperative, minimally distressed, and appears puzzled by the commotion, stating he simply forgot to pay. His wife, visibly distraught, insists this is the fourth or fifth such incident over 18 months and that her husband is 'not himself.' She is the primary historian.

Approximately 18 months ago, Mr. R — formerly a responsible warehouse supervisor known for precision and interpersonal warmth — began showing gradual but progressive behavioral changes that the family initially attributed to occupational stress. He became less emotionally engaged, rarely initiating conversations with his wife or adult children. He stopped cooking, a previously strong interest, without explanation. His colleagues at work noticed increasing impulsivity: he twice confronted coworkers with disproportionate anger over minor matters, and he was ultimately terminated for insubordination four months ago. His wife reports that he appeared relieved rather than distressed by the termination.

Over the same period, his dietary behavior has changed markedly: he craves sweet foods almost exclusively and has gained approximately 14 lbs. He watches the same two action films on a daily loop, refusing to change the routine, and arranges his shoes and wallet items in a fixed order every morning. He has made two significant financial errors of judgment — an unauthorized $6,000 wire to an online casino and an impulsive purchase of sports memorabilia — without apparent remorse or insight into the consequences.

The family reported no fever, no headache or neck stiffness, no focal weakness or sensory loss, no tremor, no falls, no hallucinations, and no seizures. There is no history of heavy alcohol use, illicit drug use, or recent medication change. His wife emphatically denies any increase in his alcohol consumption prior to this event. Tox screen ordered by police prior to transport was reported as negative.

The ED team is considering primary psychiatric diagnoses (late-onset mania, substance intoxication) and potential delirium secondary to a metabolic cause, given the acute presentation. No cognitive or structural workup has yet been initiated.

findings.finding: Executive function (DKEFS Trails, Color-Word Interference): Severely impaired. Trails switching (condition 4): 1st percentile. Color-word inhibition/switching: 3rd percentile.
Verbal fluency: Letter fluency (FAS total): 14 (12th percentile — low). Category fluency (animals): 9/60 s (impaired, <10th percentile).

Social cognition (Reading the Mind in the Eyes; Faux Pas Test): Eyes test 16/36 (<2nd percentile — severely impaired). Faux Pas: identified 2 of 10 scenarios correctly (<2nd percentile). Social cognition severely impaired.

Episodic memory (HVLT-R): Immediate recall 8/12 (35th percentile — low average). Delayed recall 6/12 (30th percentile). Recognition 11/12 (50th percentile). Memory impairment is present but not severe; recognition relatively preserved.
Working memory (WAIS-IV Digit Span): Forward 6, backward 4 — low average.
Language (BNT short form): 12/15 (35th percentile) — within normal limits for age.
Behavioral rating (informant — wife; Frontal Behavioral Inventory): FBI 33/72 — elevated, indicating clinically significant disinhibition, apathy, and perseverative behaviors.

output.impression: Neuropsychological profile: severely impaired executive function and social cognition with relative preservation of episodic memory recognition and visuospatial function. Frontal Behavioral Inventory markedly elevated per informant. Language broadly intact. Pattern of selective anterior-network impairment with posterior cortical sparing

results.title: Sensitivity of revised diagnostic criteria for the behavioural variant of frontotemporal dementia
results.finding: Rascovsky et al. 2011 criteria require ≥3 of 6 core features (behavioral disinhibition, apathy/inertia, loss of empathy, perseverative/stereotyped behaviors, hyperorality/dietary changes, executive dysfunction) within the first 3 years. 'Probable bvFTD' additionally requires functional decline plus frontotemporal atrophy or hypometabolism on neuroimaging. The criteria were designed for longitudinal outpatient cohorts but the behavioral features are often first apparent in acute or crisis settings.

results.title: Frontotemporal dementia
results.finding: Bang et al. (Lancet 2015) describe acute behavioral crises — including legal incidents, financial misconduct, and public disinhibition — as common first presentations of bvFTD that often lead to psychiatric rather than neurological assessment. Patients typically present to legal, psychiatric, or emergency settings before a neurodegenerative etiology is considered. Anchoring on acute precipitants delays correct diagnosis by a median of 3-4 years.

results.title: FDG-PET improves accuracy in distinguishing frontotemporal lobar degeneration and Alzheimer disease
results.finding: Foster et al. report FDG-PET sensitivity of 97% and specificity of 86% for distinguishing FTD from AD, particularly when MRI atrophy is early or moderate. Frontotemporal hypometabolism with posterior cingulate sparing is the hallmark pattern.

output.summary: bvFTD commonly first comes to clinical attention through behavioral crises — criminal incidents, financial misjudgments, or public disinhibition — rather than through cognitive complaints. Emergency and psychiatric settings are frequent first points of contact, where anchoring on acute psychiatric or substance-related diagnoses delays the neurodegenerative workup. Rascovsky 2011 criteria require ≥3 of 6 core behavioral features within 3 years plus functional decline; probable classification requires structural or metabolic frontotemporal abnormality. FDG-PET (Foster 2007) offers high sensitivity for frontotemporal hypometabolism when MRI atrophy is moderate.

findings.finding: Asymmetric hypometabolism involving bilateral frontal lobes, left greater than right. Left superior, middle, and inferior frontal gyri show 24-28% reduction in FDG uptake compared to cerebellar reference. Right frontal involvement milder (10-14% reduction). Bilateral orbitofrontal cortex hypometabolic.
Mild bilateral anterior temporal hypometabolism, left greater than right (12-16% reduction on left, 6-8% on right).
Preserved — posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, parietal association cortex, and occipital lobes show normal FDG uptake.
Caudate nuclei mildly hypometabolic bilaterally, left slightly more than right.

output.impression: Asymmetric left frontotemporal hypometabolism with relative posterior cortex preservation — a pattern consistent with frontotemporal hypometabolism. Posterior cingulate and precuneus uptake preserved

findings.finding: C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion: No expansion detected — 2/4 repeats (normal, <30 repeats; pathogenic typically >400 repeats).
GRN (progranulin) sequencing: No pathogenic variant identified. Common polymorphism c.1414C>T (rs5848) present — not pathogenic.
MAPT sequencing and haplotype: No pathogenic variant identified. H1/H2 haplotype — not causative.
TARDBP (TDP-43) sequencing: No pathogenic variant identified.

output.impression: No pathogenic variant identified in the FTD genetic panel (C9orf72, GRN, MAPT, TARDBP). Findings are consistent with sporadic rather than familial frontotemporal dementia etiology

differential.key_features: Acute disinhibition, impulsivity, and inappropriate behavior in a patient with no prior psychiatric history fits a first manic episode; refuted by 18-month insidious prodrome, absence of mood elevation/grandiosity/decreased sleep, and frontotemporal structural and metabolic changes.

differential.diagnosis: Substance intoxication or acute substance-related behavior
differential.key_features: Shoplifting in context of a bottle of cognac mimics intoxication; refuted by undetectable blood alcohol, negative urine tox screen, wife's denial of alcohol excess, and the 18-month behavioral prodrome preceding this incident.

differential.diagnosis: Delirium secondary to metabolic or toxic cause
differential.key_features: Acute behavioral change in ED raises delirium; refuted by normal metabolic panel (electrolytes, glucose, ammonia, creatinine, LFTs, thyroid), no fever, normal WBC, and preserved alertness and orientation.

Behavioral changes and frontal atrophy can be seen in atypical AD; differentiated by executive-predominant profile with relative memory sparing, frontotemporal rather than temporoparietal metabolic pattern, and lack of memory-predominant profile.
Hypertension and Fazekas grade 1 changes are present, but white matter burden is minor and insufficient to account for the lobar behavioral syndrome.

Subacute behavioral change in a male could raise autoimmune encephalitis concern; against: insidious 18-month course without psychiatric prodrome fluctuations, no seizures, no autonomic instability, normal CSF expected.

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD and not part of the standard behavioral dementia workup unless rapid progression raises concern for CJD or seizures are present.
ECG has no role in the workup of a behavioral dementia syndrome; reserved for cardiac symptoms or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to the diagnostic question of a neurodegenerative behavioral syndrome.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in the absence of syncope, palpitations, or arrhythmia.
DaTscan assesses presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; not indicated here because there is no parkinsonism, tremor, or features suggesting DLB or atypical parkinsonism.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.

sequence_constraints.reason: In the ED setting, CT is the initial rapid structural screen to exclude hemorrhage; MRI follows as the definitive structural characterization study.
Exclude structural cause of focal cognitive symptoms and screen for elevated ICP before lumbar puncture.

critical_actions: Resist the acute-psychiatric anchor: recognize that the ED presentation (shoplifting incident) is an acute behavioral crisis on top of a chronic 18-month neurodegenerative prodrome — not a new-onset psychiatric disorder.
Exclude reversible and acute causes first (metabolic, toxic, structural) before attributing the syndrome to neurodegeneration.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within first 3 years) using wife's collateral history, not the patient's self-report.
Ensure patient safety given ongoing disinhibition: assess capacity, restrict driving, alert family to financial safeguards and potential for further impulsive incidents.
Do not discharge from the ED to home with a primary psychiatric diagnosis without cognitive and structural workup or explicit neurology follow-up arranged.
Assess decision-making and driving capacity before discharge.
contraindicated_actions: Do not discharge from the ED with a diagnosis of substance intoxication or primary mania without pursuing a structural and cognitive workup, given the clear 18-month prodrome.
Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): not indicated in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may exacerbate agitation.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls in this population.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line therapy without specialist neurology or behavioral neurology input.
key_reasoning_points: The shoplifting arrest is the presenting symptom but the clinical problem is the 18-month behavioral prodrome: the acute incident is merely the tip of a chronic neurodegenerative syndrome that the family had minimized.

Normal metabolic panel, normal tox screen, and absence of fever rule out the three most common ED acute behavioral mimics (intoxication, delirium, metabolic encephalopathy) — the diagnosis must then pivot toward structural or primary neurological disease.

The combination of: (1) behavioral disinhibition, (2) apathy/loss of initiative, (3) loss of empathy, (4) perseverative/stereotyped behaviors, (5) hyperorality/dietary change, and (6) executive dysfunction constitutes ≥5 of the 6 Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD core features — meeting probable criteria when structural frontotemporal change is confirmed.

MMSE of 27/30 in the ED may falsely reassure: bvFTD disproportionately impairs behavior and social cognition while leaving MMSE relatively intact early — the executive subscale deficits and social cognition impairment found on formal neuropsychological testing are the discriminating measures.

The atypical ED encounter type tests whether the agent resists acute-psychiatric anchoring and recognizes that an isolated behavioral incident in a 61-year-old requires a full neurodegenerative workup before a psychiatric disposition.

red_herrings.data_point: Normal tox screen and blood alcohol level <10 mg/dL with the incident involving a bottle of cognac
red_herrings.intended_effect: A negative tox screen confirming the patient was sober might paradoxically reinforce a primary psychiatric (manic) interpretation rather than prompting a neurodegenerative workup — the ED team may reason 'this is not intoxication, so it must be mania.'
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The negative tox screen rules out acute intoxication as the cause of this incident, but it does not explain the 18-month behavioral prodrome; the correct next step is structural and cognitive workup for neurodegeneration.

red_herrings.intended_effect: A near-normal MMSE may falsely reassure the ED clinician that there is no significant cognitive impairment, supporting a primary psychiatric or volitional behavioral interpretation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: bvFTD characteristically spares MMSE-tested domains (orientation, recall, basic language) early while severely impairing executive function and social cognition, which are not captured by the MMSE; near-normal MMSE does not exclude bvFTD.

red_herrings.data_point: No family history of dementia or FTD
red_herrings.intended_effect: Absence of family history may lower the clinical suspicion for FTD, reinforcing a primary psychiatric interpretation.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Approximately 70% of bvFTD is sporadic with no identifiable family history; absence of family history is the norm rather than the exception and does not argue against bvFTD.

metadata.notes: First emergency-encounter FTD case in v5. 61-year-old Hispanic man presenting to ED after shoplifting arrest on background of 18-month bvFTD prodrome. Core teaching: resist acute-psychiatric anchoring; normal metabolic/tox workup is reassuring but does not explain the prodrome; near-normal MMSE does not exclude bvFTD; structural and cognitive workup is required before psychiatric disposition.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools (CT, labs, MRI, neuropsych, literature) plus recommended FDG-PET and genetic panel; 3 grounded red herrings (negative tox screen, near-normal MMSE, absent family history); acute ED encounter type requires resisting acute-psychiatric anchor and recognizing the chronic neurodegenerative prodrome — cross-modal synthesis of metabolic exclusion, structural imaging, and neuropsychological profile.
